# Tests of General Relativity with GW250114

On January 14th, 2025, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration detected the clearest binary black hole merger to date. Its signal to noise ratio was almost 80.

The signal is clearly visible with minimal processing: @fig-gw250114-whitened-strain-simplified shows whitened strain data (see @sec-strain-whitening) from the Hanford and Livingston detectors.

![Whitened strain for GW250114 in the Livingston and Hanford detectors. Adapted from @abacGW250114TestingHawkings2025.](figures/Figure_1_simplified.pdf){#fig-gw250114-whitened-strain-simplified width=100%}

After the first gravitational wave detection in 2015, @theligoscientificcollaborationBasicPhysicsBinary2017 gave an outline of the basic physics that can be gleamed from the "bare" data without the need to invoke complex models.

Similarly, here we can visually identify the sections of the waveform emitted by a black hole coalescence:

- an _inspiral_, whose amplitude and frequency rise over time;
- a _merger_, where the signal's amplitude peaks;
- a _ringdown_, characterized by strongly damped oscillations.

Indeed, if we overlay the general relativistic prediction for a binary merger [@fig-gw250114-whitened-strain] we can see that it matches very closely.

![Upper panel: whitened strain for GW250114 in the Livingston and Hanford detectors, along with modelled and unmodelled waveform reconstructions. Lower panel: a time-frequency spectrogram of the whitened data. Adapted from @abacGW250114TestingHawkings2025.](figures/Figure_1.pdf){#fig-gw250114-whitened-strain width=100%}

This chapter will discuss the "anatomy" of a gravitational wave signal, the way it is parameterized, and the way it appears in our detectors, using GW250114 as an example wherever possible, but also with an eye toward low frequencies, which we will then expand on in @sec-lgwa. 
The current chapter will focus on ringdown, as this is what allowed for the most prominent scientific results with GW250114. 
@sec-intrinsic will describe the intrinsic modelling of a gravitational wave signal, with parameters such the masses and spins of the two component objects, eccentricity, tidal effects.
In @sec-extrinsic we will bring the signal from source to detector, discussing the impact of precession, detector motion and antenna patterns.

## Ringdown {#sec-ringdown}

After the coalescence of two Kerr black holes, the remnant quickly settles into a quiescent state, emitting gravitational radiation in a process called _ringdown_.

![Whitened strain in the ringdown of GW250114. The data from the Hanford detector was shifted in time and inverted to account for its different position and antenna pattern.](figures/overlapped_strains.pdf){#fig-whitened-strain-ringdown-gw250114}

The qualitative behaviour of this regime is apparent in @fig-whitened-strain-ringdown-gw250114: it looks like a damped sinusoid. 

This radiation can be described, at the perturbative level, in terms of quasi-normal modes (QNMs), whose complex frequencies $\omega_{\ell mn} = 2 \pi f_{\ell mn} - i / \tau_{\ell mn}$ are well-understood functions of the black hole properties: mass $M_{f}$ and spin magnitude $\chi_{f}$.

```{python}
import qnm
import astropy.units as u
import astropy.constants as ac
import numpy as np

def get_f_tau(M, chi, l, m, n):
    q22 = qnm.modes_cache(-2, l, m, n)
    omega, _, _ = q22(a=chi)

    f = np.real(omega) / (2 * np.pi) / (ac.G * M / ac.c**3)
    tau = 1/(- np.imag(omega) / (ac.G * M / ac.c**3))
    return f.to(u.Hz), tau.to(u.ms)

M = 68.4*u.Msun
chi = 0.68
f_220, tau_220 = get_f_tau(M, chi, 2, 2, 0)

print(f'For a remnant black hole with {M=:.1f} and {chi=:.2f}')
print(f'the fundamental frequency is {f_220=:.2f}')
print(f'and the damping time is {tau_220=:.2f}.')
```

The fact that $f_{220} \approx 1/\tau_{220}$ means that the sinusoid corresponding to this mode is approximately suppressed by a factor $e$ every cycle.
This decay is comparatively slow for a mode: most other QNMs are suppressed even faster [@bertiBlackHoleSpectroscopy2025, figure 2.3].

In terms of these modes, the gravitational wave polarizations from a Kerr black hole's ringdown can be expressed as [@bertiBlackHoleSpectroscopy2025, equation 6.12]:^[This expression only considers prograde modes, which co-rotate with the remnant black hole's spin; retrograde ones are hardly excited for quasi-circular binaries.]
$$
h_{+}(t)-ih_{\times}(t) \approx \sum_{\ell'}^{\infty} \sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} A_{\ell mn} \exp(i(\omega^{x}_{\ell mn}(t-t_\text{ref})+\phi^{x}_{\ell mn})) _{(-2)}Y_{\ell mn}
$$
Predicting the amplitudes of these modes is in general hard, doing so in the generic-orbit case is in fact an open problem [@carulloBlackHoleSpectroscopy2025].

Ringdown analyses may be performed at several levels of model-dependence, ranging from a purely data-driven fit with damped sinusoids to imposing a prescription for the Kerr spectrum as well as the mode amplitudes [@bertiBlackHoleSpectroscopy2025, table 7].

In order to isolate the ringdown, one generally analyzes data starting after the coalescence, with the time domain data analysis techniques described in @sec-time-domain-pe. But what should the start time be?
The initial spacetime at the collision is highly dynamical and nonlinear, and asymptotically approaches the perturbative regime in which the QNM description is formulated. 
This is at the core of a fundamental tension in ringdown science: the perturbative assumption is better verified the further along one starts, but the signal is quickly decaying and starting too late means losing valuable data.

![Frequencies, damping times and SNRs as a function of analysis start time in the ringdown of GW250114. Adapted from @abacGW250114TestingHawkings2025.](figures/fs_gs_snrs_vs_time.pdf){#fig-gw250114-fs-gs-snrs width=100%}

In figure @fig-gw250114-fs-gs-snrs this tension is visible for GW250114: 
the horizontal axis in all panels is the analysis start time, 
expressed in units of the characteristic timescale corresponding to the 
detector-frame remnant mass, $t_{M_{f}} = (1+z) G M_{f} /c^{3} \approx 337 \upmu \text{s}$.
The SNR quickly decreases with time, 
and the errors on the measured parameters 
--- frequencies and damping times of the fundamental ringdown mode 
and its first overtone --- accordingly increase with start time.

While this problem remains here as in all ringdown analyses, 
another fact to notice in @fig-gw250114-fs-gs-snrs is the
very high magnitude of the ringdown-only SNR. 
As far as $20 t_{M_{f}}$ after the peak it is of the order of 10, 
more than the entirety of some other gravitational wave signals.

## Detection of the 221 overtone

The exceptional SNR of GW250114 allowed for the confident detection of the $\ell m n = 221$ overtone in the data. 
Its amplitude was constrained to be non-vanishing: @fig-gw250114-mode-amplitudes illustrates posterior distributions on the amplitudes of the 220 and 221. 
There is a temporal window, between 6 and 8 $t_{M_{f}}$ after the peak, during which the overtone amplitude is constrained to be larger than 0 at more than $3 \sigma$.

![Posterior distributions for the amplitudes of the fundamental and first overtone of GW250114. Adapted from @abacGW250114TestingHawkings2025.](figures/spectroscopy_10.5M.pdf){#fig-gw250114-mode-amplitudes}

The grey bands in the figure indicate the theoretical expectation for the exponential decay of the two modes. 
They are obtained by considering the posterior samples at the reference time for that analysis ($6 t_{M_{f}}$ for the 221, $10.5t_{M_{f}}$ for the 220), and evolving them backward and forward in time according to their respective amplitude and decay time.
The grey band is then computed by considering the HPD intervals with 50 and 90% credibility (see @sec-credible-regions).

### Spectroscopic test of the Kerr metric

The confident detection of a 221 overtone enabled a spectroscopic test of General Relativity: 
we performed an analysis which constrained the two ringdown tones to their values with the Kerr metric, but also allowed for a deviation in the frequency and damping rate of the 221 tone:
$$
f_{221} = e^{\delta f_{221}} f_{221}^{\text{Kerr}}
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
\gamma_{221} = e^{\delta \gamma_{221}} \gamma_{221}^{\text{Kerr}}\,.
$$

This allowed the two modes to freely vary, independently of each other.
In the right panel of @fig-spectroscopy we show the posterior distribution on the deviation parameter $\delta f_{221}$: it is constrained to be close to zero, a null result.
The left panel offers an alternative perspective on the same result: we show the two-dimensional posterior distribution on the frequencies $(1+z)f_{220}$ and $(1+z)f_{221}$.^[The quantities in the plot are the measured frequencies at the detector. Due to cosmological effects we expect them to be redshifted by a factor $(1+z)$ - see also @sec-distance-redshift.]
The grey diagonal band shows the range of possible combinations of values under the Kerr assumption. 
They change as a function of detector-frame remnant mass $(1+z)M_{f}$ and spin $\chi_{f}$; these are free parameters in the ringdown analysis, hence the wide posterior. 
However, if we were to use the whole signal as opposed to only its ringdown, we would get values near the black cross.

![Spectroscopic test of the 221 QNM's frequency with GW250114. Adapted from @abacGW250114TestingHawkings2025.](figures/221_kerr_test.pdf){#fig-spectroscopy}

## Area law

The possibility to independently analyze the inspiral and ringdown also provided the opportunity to validate Hawking's area law: the statement that the horizon area of black holes in the universe must increase over time. 

In the context of a binary coalescence, this translates to the statement that the remnant area should be larger than the sum of the component areas: 
$$
A_{1} + A_{2} \leq A_{f}\,.
$$

The surface area of a Kerr black hole is given in terms of its mass $M$ and spin magnitude $\chi$ by:
$$ A(M, \chi) = 8 \pi \left(  \frac{GM}{c^{2}} \right)^{2} \left( 1+\sqrt{ 1-\chi^{2} } \right) \,.
$$
The inspiral and ringdown analyses do not directly give us access to the mass $M$ of the black holes: instead, the signal directly depends on detector frame masses, in the form $(1+z)M$ --- see @sec-distance-redshift.
Fortunately, this does not pose a problem for this analysis, as the ratio $(A_{f} - A_{1} - A_{2}) / (A_{1} + A_{2})$ is independent of the signal's redshift.

![Posterior distribution for the fractional area change of GW250114. Adapted from @abacGW250114TestingHawkings2025.](figures/area_law_plot_combined.pdf)
